title: Double Electrophilic Borylative Cyclization of a Pyridine Core Enables a Narrowband Ultraviolet B/N/O MR-TADF Emitter
authors: Yue Wang; Jie Li; Zhangli Cheng; Xi Zhang; Maike Lin; Lingwei Qu; Zebin Chen; Kai Wang; Jun Ye
abstract: Abstract A pyridine-embedded boron/nitrogen/oxygen multiple-resonance emitter, tBuBOPy, was synthesized on gram scale via methoxy-directed tandem borylation at the pyridine C3 and C5 positions. The incorporation of pyridine blue-shifts the emission by preferentially stabilizing the highest occupied molecular orbital. It also modifies the excited-state character, reducing hole–electron overlap and lowering the singlet–triplet energy gap. As a result, tBuBOPy exhibits ultraviolet TADF at 383 nm, with an fwhm of 25 nm and a high PLQY of 89%.

title: Crack-driven electrical response in stretchable electronics: an original multi-scale characterization
authors: Marie Goizet; Raphaël Passas; Guillaume Krosnicki; Julien Bras; Aurore Denneulin
abstract: Abstract Emerging applications in electronics require devices capable of conforming to complex three-dimensional geometries, such as wearable systems. Stretchable electronics must remain functional under mechanical deformation. In this work, stretchable conductive inks with innovative formulation are proposed, using silver flakes as the conductive material and bio-based binders, namely hydroxypropylmethyl cellulose (HPMC) and TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanofibrils (CNFt). The choice of binder significantly influences the stretchability of the printed conductive tracks and the crack formation under strain. To investigate the initiation and evolution of microcracks over deformations, we employ an original experimental approach combining in-situ scanning electron microscopy tensile testing with direct observation of microstructural evolution. This technique provides key insights into the underlying mechanisms governing crack pattern formation under realistic loading conditions. The results show that HPMC promotes the formation of a limited number of large cracks, whereas CNFt leads to the formation of numerous thin cracks. Combining both binder materials enables control over crack formation (morphology and distribution). This is critical, as microstructural evolution under strain is the predominant factor governing the relative change in electrical resistance. Overall, this approach establishes a powerful methodology for linking microstructural evolution to functional electrical performance, thereby enabling the rational design of highly reliable stretchable conductive materials.
